questions.question: What was the traditional subject matter of ukiyo-e before Hokusai helped broaden the style?
options: portraiture focused on courtesans and actors
landscapes, plants, and animals
European-style engravings
religious scenes and calligraphy
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states that ukiyo-e was 'a style of portraiture largely focused on courtesans and actors' before Hokusai developed it into a broader style.
Incorrect. Landscapes, plants, and animals were the broader focus Hokusai introduced, not the traditional subject matter.
Incorrect. European styles were explored later by Hokusai, but they were not the traditional ukiyo-e subjects.
Incorrect. The article does not identify religious scenes and calligraphy as the traditional focus of ukiyo-e.

questions.question: Which two prints from the Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji series are specifically credited with securing Hokusai's fame in Japan and overseas?
options: The Great Wave off Kanagawa and Fine Wind, Clear Morning
The Great Wave off Kanagawa and Red Fuji
Fine Wind, Clear Morning and One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji
The Great Wave off Kanagawa and The Dream of the Fisherman's Wife
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states that 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa and Fine Wind, Clear Morning' secured his fame both in Japan and overseas.
Incorrect. Red Fuji is mentioned as part of the series, but the article specifically names Fine Wind, Clear Morning alongside The Great Wave as securing his fame.
Incorrect. One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji is a different series produced later, not one of the prints credited with securing his fame.
Incorrect. The Dream of the Fisherman's Wife is a shunga work, not part of the Thirty-Six Views series credited with his fame.

questions.question: What event did Hokusai describe as inspirational to the development of his artistic style?
options: the embarrassment he suffered at ShunkÅ's hands
the death of his master Katsukawa ShunshÅ
his expulsion from the Tawaraya School
a fire that destroyed his studio in 1839
answer_explanations: Correct. Hokusai is quoted as saying, 'What really motivated the development of my artistic style was the embarrassment I suffered at ShunkÅ's hands.'
Incorrect. ShunshÅ's death prompted Hokusai to explore other styles, but he specifically credited the embarrassment at ShunkÅ's hands as motivating his style.
Incorrect. The article mentions expulsion from the Katsukawa school by ShunkÅ, not the Tawaraya School.
Incorrect. The 1839 fire occurred much later and is not described as inspirational to his artistic development.

questions.question: What does the name 'Katsushika Hokusai' refer to, according to the article?
options: the part of Edo where he was born and 'north studio' in honour of the North Star
his childhood name TokitarÅ and his father's mirror-making trade
the Katsukawa school and a Buddhist deity
the Honjo district and a nickname given by his master ShunshÅ
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states the former name refers to the part of Edo where he was born, and the latter means 'north studio', in honour of the North Star.
Incorrect. TokitarÅ was his childhood name, and his father was a mirror-maker, but neither is part of the name Katsushika Hokusai.
Incorrect. The Katsukawa school was his master's school, and Nichiren Buddhism is mentioned in connection with the North Star, but these are not what the name refers to.
Incorrect. The Honjo district is mentioned in an account of his birth, and ShunshÅ gave him the name ShunrÅ, but neither explains Katsushika Hokusai.

questions.question: What did Hokusai create during an Edo festival in 1804?
options: an enormous portrait of the Buddhist prelate Daruma
a blue curve with red chicken footprints across it
the first volume of Hokusai Manga
One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states that during an Edo festival in 1804, he created an enormous portrait of Daruma, said to be 200 square meters.
Incorrect. The chicken-footprint painting was created at the court of the shÅgun, not during the Edo festival.
Incorrect. The first volume of Hokusai Manga was published in 1814, not created at the 1804 festival.
Incorrect. One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji was produced beginning in 1834, not in 1804.

questions.question: Why did Hokusai write to blockcutters during the production of Toshisen Ehon?
options: to request amendments so the prints would be true to his style
to end his collaboration with Takizawa Bakin
to commission illustrations for Hokusai Manga
to complain about the publisher's payment terms
answer_explanations: Correct. Hokusai wrote to blockcutters because they had strayed from his style and he stated amendments were needed for the final prints to be true to his style.
Incorrect. The collaboration with Takizawa Bakin ended earlier and for different reasons, such as discordant personalities.
Incorrect. Hokusai Manga was a separate project begun later, not commissioned through letters to blockcutters.
Incorrect. The article does not mention payment terms as the subject of his letters.

questions.question: What was the purpose of Hokusai's etehon, or art manuals, beginning with Quick Lessons in Simplified Drawing?
options: to make money and attract more students
to record his deathbed haiku
to compete with AndÅ Hiroshige
to replace woodblock printing with painting
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states these manuals 'were intended as a convenient way to make money and attract more students.'
Incorrect. The deathbed haiku is mentioned separately at the end of the article, not as the purpose of the manuals.
Incorrect. Hiroshige became popular later as Hokusai's career faded, but the manuals were not created to compete with him.
Incorrect. The article does not suggest the manuals were intended to replace woodblock printing.

questions.question: Which series did Hokusai produce under the name 'GakyÅ RÅjin Manji'?
options: One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji
Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji
Hokusai Manga
One Hundred Poems Explained by a Nurse
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states that under the name GakyÅ RÅjin Manji, beginning in 1834, he produced One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji.
Incorrect. Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji was produced earlier under the name Iitsu, in the early 1830s.
Incorrect. Hokusai Manga was produced during the Taito period beginning in 1811.
Incorrect. One Hundred Poems Explained by a Nurse was his final print series, produced around 1835 to 1836, not under the name GakyÅ RÅjin Manji.

questions.question: What did Hokusai reportedly exclaim on his deathbed?
options: If only Heaven will give me just another ten years... Just another five more years, then I could become a real painter
Though as a ghost, I shall lightly tread, the summer fields
What really motivated the development of my artistic style was the embarrassment I suffered at ShunkÅ's hands
At one hundred and ten, each dot, each line will possess a life of its own
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states he apparently exclaimed on his deathbed, 'If only Heaven will give me just another ten years... Just another five more years, then I could become a real painter.'
Incorrect. The ghost haiku was composed shortly before his death, but it is not the deathbed exclamation described in the article.
Incorrect. This quotation about embarrassment at ShunkÅ's hands refers to his artistic motivation, not his deathbed words.
Incorrect. This line comes from the colophon to One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji, not his deathbed exclamation.

questions.question: What happened to Hokusai's studio and much of his work in 1839?
options: a fire destroyed them
they were sold to Vincent van Gogh
they were donated to the British Museum
they were seized by the Tokugawa shogunate
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states that in 1839, a fire destroyed Hokusai's studio and much of his work.
Incorrect. Van Gogh was influenced by Hokusai's works, but the article does not say the studio was sold to him.
Incorrect. The Great Picture Book of Everything is in the British Museum, but the studio was not donated there.
Incorrect. The article does not mention the Tokugawa shogunate seizing his studio or work.
